subject: Augustus
overview: Born Gaius Octavius, the great-nephew of Julius Caesar, Augustus was a sickly teenager when Caesar's murder made him heir to a name and a fortune, and he used both to fight his way to sole control of the Roman world. As Rome's first emperor, from 27 BC until his death in AD 14, he kept the old Republic's offices and titles in place while holding the real power himself, and his reign opened two centuries of relative peace across the Mediterranean known as the Pax Romana.

key_moments.title: Named heir in Caesar's will
key_moments.text: When **Julius Caesar** was stabbed to death in the Senate on the Ides of March, his will held a surprise: he had **adopted his great-nephew Octavius** as his son and left him the bulk of his estate. Octavius, then studying in Apollonia across the Adriatic, sailed back to Italy against his family's advice and took the name **Gaius Julius Caesar**. Seasoned politicians like **Mark Antony** and **Cicero** dismissed him as a useful boy, but he paid Caesar's promised bequests to the Roman people out of his own pocket and raised a private army of Caesar's veterans. He was **just 18 years old**.
claims: Julius Caesar was assassinated in 44 BC.
Julius Caesar's will adopted Gaius Octavius as his son and named him his main heir.
Octavius was in Apollonia when Julius Caesar was assassinated.
Octavius was 18 years old when Julius Caesar was assassinated.

key_moments.title: Second Triumvirate and the proscriptions
key_moments.text: After first fighting Mark Antony, Octavian switched sides and joined him and **Marcus Aemilius Lepidus** in the **Second Triumvirate**, a three-man dictatorship given legal force by the Senate. The three men drew up **proscription lists** of enemies who could be killed and whose property was seized, partly to pay their armies. In 42 BC they crushed Caesar's assassins **Brutus and Cassius** at **Philippi**. The most famous victim of the lists was **Cicero**, who had praised and promoted the young Octavian only months earlier.
claims: Octavian, Mark Antony and Marcus Aemilius Lepidus formed the Second Triumvirate in 43 BC.
The Second Triumvirate issued proscriptions that led to killings and property confiscations.
Cicero was killed in 43 BC as a victim of the proscriptions.
Octavian and Mark Antony defeated Brutus and Cassius at the Battle of Philippi in 42 BC.

key_moments.title: Victory at Actium
key_moments.text: The partnership with Antony collapsed into war, which Octavian framed as Rome against the Egyptian queen **Cleopatra**, Antony's ally and lover. Off the coast of western Greece, at the **Battle of Actium**, Octavian's fleet under his friend **Marcus Agrippa** defeated the combined navy of Antony and Cleopatra. A year later, as Octavian's army closed in on **Alexandria**, both took their own lives. Egypt, the richest kingdom left in the Mediterranean, became a **Roman province** governed as the personal domain of Octavian, and its grain helped feed the city of Rome.
claims: The Battle of Actium was fought in 31 BC off the coast of western Greece.
Marcus Agrippa commanded Octavian's fleet at the Battle of Actium.
Mark Antony and Cleopatra died by suicide in Alexandria in 30 BC.
Egypt was annexed as a Roman province after the deaths of Mark Antony and Cleopatra.

key_moments.title: The Senate names him Augustus
key_moments.text: In a carefully staged session, Octavian announced he was **handing his powers back to the Senate and people of Rome**. The Senate responded by granting him control of the key frontier provinces and their armies, and a new honorific name: **Augustus**, meaning roughly "the revered one." He called himself **princeps**, "first citizen," rather than king, and over the following decades he rebuilt temples, reorganised the army and the provinces, and set up a standing guard. He later boasted, according to the biographer **Suetonius**, that he had found Rome a city of brick and left it a city of marble.
claims: In 27 BC the Roman Senate granted Octavian the name Augustus.
In 27 BC Octavian formally returned his powers to the Senate and people of Rome.
Augustus used the title princeps rather than king.
Suetonius reports that Augustus boasted he found Rome a city of brick and left it a city of marble.

deep_facts.text: The month of **August** was renamed from Sextilis in his honour in 8 BC, because it was the month of several of his greatest successes, including the fall of Alexandria. A popular story claims that Augustus, jealous of Julius Caesar's July, stole a day from February so that his month would not be shorter. The tale is a medieval invention, usually traced to the 13th-century scholar **Johannes de Sacrobosco**: Sextilis already had 31 days before it was ever renamed.
claims: The Roman month Sextilis was renamed August in honour of Augustus in 8 BC.
A story exists that Augustus took a day from February to make August as long as July.
The story about August taking a day from February is usually attributed to Johannes de Sacrobosco in the 13th century.
Sextilis already had 31 days before it was renamed August.

deep_facts.text: In AD 9, three Roman legions under **Publius Quinctilius Varus** were wiped out in the Teutoburg Forest by Germanic tribes led by Arminius, a chief who had served in the Roman army. Suetonius describes the elderly emperor going for months without cutting his hair or beard and sometimes beating his head against a door while crying out, "Quinctilius Varus, give me back my legions!" The numbers of the lost legions, XVII, XVIII and XIX, were never used again.
claims: Three Roman legions under Publius Quinctilius Varus were destroyed in the Battle of the Teutoburg Forest in AD 9.
Arminius led the Germanic forces at the Battle of the Teutoburg Forest.
Suetonius reports that Augustus cried out for Quinctilius Varus to give back his legions.
The legion numbers XVII, XVIII and XIX were never used again by the Roman army.

deep_facts.text: Augustus wrote his own account of his achievements, the **Res Gestae Divi Augusti**, and ordered it inscribed on bronze pillars outside his mausoleum in Rome. Those bronze originals are lost. The most complete text survives far from Rome, carved in Latin and Greek on the walls of a temple to Rome and Augustus in **Ankyra, modern Ankara in Turkey**, which is why scholars still call it the Monumentum Ancyranum.
claims: Augustus wrote the Res Gestae Divi Augusti as an account of his achievements.
The Res Gestae Divi Augusti was meant to be inscribed on bronze pillars at the Mausoleum of Augustus.
The most complete surviving copy of the Res Gestae Divi Augusti is on the Temple of Augustus and Rome in Ankara.
The Ankara copy of the Res Gestae Divi Augusti is inscribed in both Latin and Greek.

connections.name: Julius Caesar
connections.connection: His great-uncle, who adopted him in his will and made him his main heir in 44 BC.

connections.name: Mark Antony
connections.connection: Fellow triumvir turned rival, defeated by him at Actium in 31 BC.

connections.name: Cleopatra
connections.connection: Queen of Egypt whom he declared war on; her death in 30 BC let him annex Egypt.

connections.name: Marcus Vipsanius Agrippa
connections.connection: His closest friend and general, who commanded his fleet at Actium and married his daughter Julia.

connections.name: Tiberius
connections.connection: His stepson, adopted in AD 4, who succeeded him as emperor in AD 14.

connections.name: Livia
connections.connection: His wife of more than fifty years and the mother of his successor Tiberius.

connections.name: Battle of Actium
connections.connection: The naval victory in 31 BC that left him sole master of the Roman world.

connections.name: Roman Empire
connections.connection: He became its first emperor in 27 BC, ending the Roman Republic in all but name.

connections.name: Cicero
connections.connection: Backed the young Octavian against Antony, then was killed in the triumvirs' proscriptions in 43 BC.

connections.name: Marcus Aemilius Lepidus
connections.connection: The third triumvir, stripped of his power by Octavian in 36 BC.

connections.name: Battle of the Teutoburg Forest
connections.connection: The loss of three legions in AD 9 that ended his plans to push the frontier to the Elbe.

connections.name: Virgil
connections.connection: Poet of his circle whose Aeneid celebrated Rome's origins and Augustus's line.
